<Rep. Mark Takano>: Committee Democrats appreciate that this bill is intended to address concerns regarding financial and budgetary management at the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA); however, there are serious issues and risks with centralizing all budget and finance employees under the Chief Financial Officer (CFO).
Committee Democrats also warn this Committee against giving tacit approval to VA to consolidate financial, acquisition, and programmatic activities for VA within a single office. Since the beginning of the second Trump administration, the President's appointee and current CFO, Richard Topping, has begun consolidating financial, acquisition, and programmatic functions within his office without any accountability to Congress. This power consolidation creates a serious conflict of interest pertaining to the oversight and award of large sums of VA funding to outside entities. The conflict of interest is apparent as Mr. Topping has taken over one of VA's most significant procurement activities. The current CFO, and not VA healthcare or acquisition officials, is leading the Community Care Network Next Generation Contract award process--a nearly $1 trillion procurement rife with issues.
In May 2026, Committee staff were briefed by Mark Englebaum, the Assistant Secretary for the Office of Human Resources and Administration, that VA must start shifting to a more aggressive planning cycle for the Department's budget for staffing, infrastructure, and other resources. That type of planning requires stability, which is often provided by career VA staff, not political appointees. These career staff are often the ones who have spent years in the Department, and know the intricacies of VA's numerous programs, its governance structures, and its employees. This is the kind of knowledge base we should be encouraging in an office such as this. While political appointees may have a role in transmitting the President's wishes as it relates to the budget, the over-politicization of planning and financial management is concerning.
At the full Committee markup on May 14, 2026, Ranking Member Takano (D-CA) offered an amendment that would have supported Mr. Englebaum's goals by restricting the number of political appointees within the Legislative and Congressional Budget Information (LCBI) office that is established in H.R. 7683. Over the last nearly year and a half, there has been a rise in the number of political appointees serving in roles traditionally held by career staff, followed by a subsequent decrease in the accessibility of information to veterans, Congress, and the public. Limiting the number of political appointees serves as a protection of processes that should be nonpartisan, including VA fiscal management. Unfortunately, this amendment failed by a recorded vote, with 10 ayes and 12 noes.
Additionally, the text of this bill creates conflicts with another bill that the majority is moving forward, Representative Barrett's H.R. 6833, the Acquisition Review and Cost Assessment Act, or ARCA, which is a bipartisan Committee priority. If both bills were to become law, they will create conflicts that would make implementation difficult, if not impossible due to how each bill alters authorities for acquisition officials within the agency. During the Oversight and Investigation Subcommittee's consideration of H.R. 7683 on March 25, 2026, concerns were raised about reconciling this bill with H.R. 6833 before consideration of either bill proceeds. Ranking Member Delia Ramirez (D-IL) encouraged a bipartisan effort to work with the Senate sponsor of H.R. 6833, Senator Jerry Moran (R-KS), to deconflict the text. To date, those negotiations have not occurred.
Another amendment, which was offered by Representative Ramirez at the full Committee markup, would have required the Department to report to Congress facility-level attrition data that Committee Democrats have requested since early 2025. The report would have included, for each employee that separated with the Department between January 1, 2025, and the enactment of this bill:
<ctr-circle> Occupation;
<ctr-circle> Job title;
<ctr-circle> Grade level;
<ctr-circle> Name and location of facility;
<ctr-circle> Reason for separation;
<ctr-circle> Whether the employee was retirement-
eligible;
<ctr-circle> Whether the employee participated in the
Deferred Resignation Program (DRP);
<ctr-circle> Whether the employee was terminated; and
<ctr-circle> Whether the position that was vacated by
the employee was eliminated by any such agency action.
This information would provide Members of the Committee critical information about the current state of the challenges facilities are facing in terms of workforce, especially as veterans begin feeling the impacts of the deferred resignation program and the voluntary early retirement authority.
Chairman Bost's rebuttal that the CFO functions--the position under which this bill intends to consolidate much of VA's financial power--are not related to the state of VA's staffing reflects a concerning trend in the Committee's oversight of this administration. Staffing makes up a significant portion of VA's $448 billion budget. To assert that this Committee does not need to know detailed information regarding staffing at the second largest federal agency is dangerous and exhibits a blatant lack of understanding regarding the budgetary functions this bill seeks to codify. Committee Democrats further argued that as VA embarks on the trillion-dollar acquisition for the Community Care Next Generation contract under CFO Topping's leadership, it is critical that we understand how VA staffing levels may impact referrals to outside care and the ongoing Republican-led privatization of VA. This amendment failed by a recorded vote, with 10 ayes and 12 noes.
Finally, on May 29, 2026, the Office of Management and Budget issued a Notice of Proposed Rule Making (NPRM) for the Proposed Federal Financial Assistance Rule, which would list the VA CFO as the official-in-charge of implementing that rule, if it becomes final. This rule would give unprecedented power to political appointees, and ultimately to the VA CFO, a veto over any science that conflicts with the current administration's ideology. The expansion of CFO power authorized in H.R. 7683 and this proposed rulemaking are concerning and unprecedented, and Committee Democrats hold that any increase in authority must be coupled with heightened oversight and accountability measures, which this legislation lacks.
Committee Democrats will continue to advocate for improving VA's fiscal operations but will reject proposals that politicize the Department's financial decision-making. Rather than improving accountability, this legislation would concentrate more power in the hands of political appointees, inviting greater political interference in VA's fiscal stewardship at the expense of veterans.
Mark Takano,
Ranking Member.
